news.title: Searching for distant planets with Astra
news.summary_raw: See how two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to find potential exoplanets in public data from NASA’s Kepler and TESS space telescopes.
news.source_text:
Searching for distant planets with Astra
Two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely.
Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system(opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992(opens in a new window). A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers.
Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope(opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90(opens in a new window).
Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars.
Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission.
One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit shows up as a dip. If the dip keeps coming back at regular intervals, astronomers know when to watch for it again.
Searching for that pattern across thousands of stars is partly a coding problem. Astronomers have published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips in years of measurements. Bond used Codex to compare those methods, combine them in a search program, and t
news.summary: OpenAI’s Codex and Astra were used by amateur astronomers to sift through Kepler telescope data, identifying new exoplanet candidates that are now under review by professional scientists. This demonstrates how AI can process massive astronomical datasets, offering a model for large-scale data analysis in other domains.

news.title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
news.source_text:
Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
TL;DR
Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.
Introduction
A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.
NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.
1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab
For simulation and training, prepare:
- A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements. 
- Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager. 
For physical-robot testing, prepare:
- A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task. 
- A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded. 
- A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles. 
Quick install
Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:
git lfs install
git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git
cd IsaacLab
uv sync --frozen
Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:
uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets
Download the walking policy
Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.
uv run isaaclab play \
  --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
  --rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \
  --num_envs 1 --visualizer none \
  --video newton_gl --video_length 1 \
  presets=backlash
2. Build the obstacle course
The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box, office bin, bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.
uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \
  --repo-type data
news.summary: NVIDIA’s Isaac Lab now offers a ready‑made Sim2Real workflow for adding obstacle avoidance to the Microduck robot using Newton’s physics engine and ToF sensing. The tutorial walks through training an avoidance controller while reusing the existing walking policy, then exporting the policy for real‑robot deployment.
news.enterprise_use: Watch for opportunities to apply Isaac Lab’s simulation training to other robotics projects you support. The workflow demonstrates how to keep core policies unchanged while adding new behavior, which could reduce the time and cost of on‑site testing for your device fleet. Evaluate whether your current SSO and endpoint security tooling can integrate with the new simulation environments to streamline onboarding of robot‑related users.

news.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police
news.summary_raw: Nvidia’s place at the center of the US economy may have outweighed concerns about its CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, national security and foreign policy experts say.
news.source_text:
Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.
Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.
President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.
The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.
Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.
“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”
Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.

news.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
news.summary_raw: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
news.source_text:
GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
- Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. 
- An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. 
- In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. 
- The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. 
In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.
Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.
Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.
Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.
Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. news.summary: OpenAI has unveiled GPT‑6 models that can autonomously design new protein structures and amino‑acid sequences, outperforming specialized biology models on several tasks. The models use reasoning and code generation, enabling researchers to guide designs with natural language prompts.

news.title: How Intentful uses dots to make more time for growth
news.summary_raw: Marina Petrova’s dot Aria helps research websites and build proposals, while proactively flagging messages and resolving issues.
news.source_text:
How Intentful uses dots to make more time for growth
How a small business founder’s dot helps her with research and proposals, while alerting her to critical messages and resolving issues.
Marina Petrova is CEO and cofounder of Intentful(opens in a new window), a lean team that helps brands make their marketing interactive, with products such as ads that answer customers’ questions in real time and tools that make website information readable by AI. The company also advises and trains marketers on using AI.
In travel and tourism, Intentful works with destination organizations and local businesses such as hotels, restaurants, and attractions. A custom proposal is part of how Marina wins their business, showing prospects what’s possible and what it would take to deliver.
To keep Intentful growing, she needed more room for that strategic work, but she was spending too much time on research, hunting for files, and formatting decks. Her dot changed all that, taking on tasks and meeting Marina’s needs before she even had to ask.
“My dot makes me feel like I gained a new superpower.”
For one of Intentful’s tourism clients, Marina wanted to propose a package of Intentful’s AI services for hundreds of local businesses in the destination. Before she could price the package, she needed to work out which businesses’ websites the package could cover and what Intentful had charged other clients for similar work.
She brought in her dot, which she named Aria, to help her get from research to a proposal she could put her name on in a few hours instead of several days. First, Marina gave Aria a spreadsheet of URLs and criteria for deciding which sites to include. For example, a site needed a readable sitemap listing no more than 3,000 pages.
“My dot looked through about 300 website sitemaps, helped me figure out which sites to include in a new offer for local businesses, and pulled pricing from past agreements.”
Next, Aria helped Marina research pricing. Through ChatGPT(opens in a new window) plugins, Aria reviewed Intentful’s sales data, including past engagements and discussions in HubSpot. It surfaced pricing from earlier agreements and context from Intentful’s plans for the following year.
Using that data, Marina and Aria then built a pricing model: page counts determined the pricing tier, and previous customer agreements also informed the price. “We worked through a custom pricing model together, and then Aria turned it into a one-page proposal I reviewed and edited,” said Marina.
When drafting proposals, Aria knows to use Intentful’s templates from Google Drive. Marina can also point Aria to an earlier proposal as a reference, so the draft follows Intentful’s style from the start. “I need to say what needs to be in a proposal, but I don’t need to spend an hour figuring out its layout. My dot handles that,” Marina says.

The dot, named Aria, pulls data from web sitemaps, sales records in HubSpot, and Google Drive templates, streamlining content creation for its tourism clients.

news.title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
news.summary_raw: The Nvidia founder apologized to his staff on Tuesday and said he was grateful for a second chance to lead the company.
news.source_text:
After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man.
Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.”
The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff.
“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added.
The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct, which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.”
Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company.
The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The president reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role
Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes.
Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.
news.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang held an all‑hands meeting where he apologized for violating the company's code of conduct and discussed his personal issues and the political support that facilitated his return. He emphasized that the code remains in force and that mitigating circumstances will be considered.

news.title: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return
news.summary_raw: The Nvidia CEO opened up about his personal life, defended his reinstatement, and acknowledged that his intense management style had hurt his staff.
news.source_text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the company’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.
During his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the company’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two children and prompted him to resign. But he said Nvidia’s board of directors made the appropriate decision for the company in welcoming him back. He added that the board made that call, not “the highest levels of our government.”
Huang spoke for about an hour, offering deeply personal thoughts about his therapy sessions and drawing applause at times from employees at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters as he spoke about the company’s success and future. He didn’t take any questions. While some Nvidia employees celebrated Huang’s return, others remained concerned about his behavior and the board’s decision to reinstate him.
“This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said as he began to speak. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.”
Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation earlier this month, citing concerns about his personal behavior and lack of candor following news reports about extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. The very same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days later, after receiving fresh assurances from Huang and learning from the Trump administration that he was not under federal criminal scrutiny and his return would not be a risk to national security.
Huang and Nvidia, though, continue to face other legal and regulatory challenges. The board is investigating whether he was the target of foreign intelligence. US lawmakers expect him to testify before Congress next week. Lawsuits and other probes are ongoing into Nvidia’s disclosures about Huang’s behavior and its compliance with US export controls on chips.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Huang told staffers that he has been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it’s “been helping me a lot.” He added that he “made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.”
While Huang said he had never knowingly made a decision contrary to the company’s interests, he conceded that “in this one area” he had lacked “the courage” to disclose information that he knew would hurt his family, seemingly referring to the extramarital affairs.

news.title: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
news.summary_raw: It's a remarkable stance for a company that spent the last two weeks finding out what happens without its founder.
news.source_text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media.
The topic of succession planning also came up — a particularly sticky issue seen as a key risk at Nvidia. Huang reportedly told staff that Nvidia doesn’t require succession planning because of its unique business model, CNBC reported, citing an unnamed source who was present. Surprisingly, given the events of the last two weeks, Huang argued that a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy.
Investors and analysts saw the issue differently earlier this month, when Huang resigned as CEO following his admission that he had extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy.
Nvidia is a flat organization, unlike other large corporations that have a swath of C-suite executives and multiple layers of management. Huang sits at the top and says he has about 60 direct reports. Nvidia has just five executive officers running the show, including Huang. The other four are CFO Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 12 days; Ajay Puri, who heads worldwide field operations; Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations; and Timothy Teter, executive vice president and general counsel, according to the company’s regulatory filings.
Huang has previously defended the company’s structure in numerous interviews, including one in March with podcaster Lex Fridman.
“When you’re designing a company, you should first think about what is it that you want the company to produce,” Huang said in the interview. “You know, I see a lot of companies’ organization charts, and they all look the same. Hamburger [company] organization charts, software organization charts, and car company organization charts. They all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. You know, the goal of company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output. And that output is the product that we like to create.”
Huang’s comments to staff, and his previous remarks on the topic of succession, may not be enough to assuage the board or shareholders over the long term, however.
news.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reiterated that the company does not need a succession plan, emphasizing a flat organizational structure during an all-hands meeting. His comments follow recent leadership turmoil and aim to maintain a streamlined hierarchy.
news.enterprise_use: Check your organization’s succession planning and hierarchy structure to ensure it aligns with your strategic goals; avoid unnecessary layers that could impede agility.

news.title: Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://www.ed.ac.uk/news/heart-attack-and-stroke-risk-detectable-decades-in-advance
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50635271
Points: 146
# Comments: 57
news.source_text:
Scientists identified early patterns in a range of risk factors for cardiovascular disease – conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels – including high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney function.
They also revealed differences in the blood of those who went on to have a cardiovascular event, such as a heart attack or stroke, more than a decade beforehand.
The findings highlight a large window of opportunity to intervene to reduce cardiovascular risk and prevent the development of serious disease, experts say.
Disease risk
Cardiovascular disease kills one in four people in the UK. Traditional risk factors, such as high blood pressure and cholesterol, have been widely linked to the risk of disease. However, previous studies have typically focused on a single risk factor and don’t monitor long-term changes.
Other influences, such as kidney function and biomarkers in the blood, could also play an important role in establishing disease risk.
A research team, led by the University of Edinburgh, examined data from more than 100,000 people between 1985 and 2019 to explore the patterns of multiple risk factors in relation to cardiovascular events over time.
The research, funded by the British Heart Foundation, included data from four population studies across the United States, Norway and the United Kingdom.
Blood pressure
Systolic blood pressure – the pressure in arteries when the heart beats or contracts – was consistently higher in those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who were event-free, starting at 4 mmHg higher three decades before and increasing to 7 mmHg closer to the event.
Patterns were different between sexes throughout life. Younger women had lower blood pressure than younger men, but this switched around the age of 65, when female readings tended to be higher than males.
Other patterns
Researchers also identified important differences by age. Those who experienced a cardiovascular event at a younger age were more likely to have diabetes and a higher body mass index in the decades before the event.
Patterns in blood biomarkers also revealed early differences between those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who didn’t. Changes in the levels of a protein called NT-proBNP – used to monitor heart failure – could be seen up to 10 years beforehand.
Trajectories of other non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including physical activity and kidney function, also differed between individuals with and without cardiovascular events.
Predict risk
Tracking the course of risk factors over time may help to better predict serious cardiovascular events, experts say. Further research should also explore whether incorporating non-traditional risk factors could help to improve the estimation of cardiovascular disease risk, they add.
The study did not look at risk factors by ethnicity, and the team cautions that further research exploring potential differences in risk factor and biom
news.summary: Scientists have discovered that patterns in cardiovascular risk factors, including blood pressure, diabetes, and kidney function, can predict heart attacks and strokes up to a decade before they occur. The study analyzed data from over 100,000 people across multiple countries and identified early biomarkers that could improve risk assessment.

news.title: State AGs fight Character AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats
news.summary_raw: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.
news.source_text:
What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.
Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.
The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.
Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)
Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.
The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.
In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.
“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.
“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”
Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”

news.summary: State attorneys general are blocking Character.ai’s plan to auction off millions of private chat logs during its bankruptcy proceedings. The move aims to prevent the sale of sensitive user data, including minors’ conversations, to a private bidder, amid new chatbot safety laws coming into effect.

news.title: Verifiable Social Reasoning for LLM Assistants
news.summary_raw: Generative AI
news.source_text:
November 25, 2026
Zorik Gekhman, Senior Research Scientist; Amir Taubenfeld, Staff Research Engineer; Google Research
We introduce an evaluation framework based on multi-agent social simulations that quantifies how well AI assistants understand social situations from users' subjective narratives. In our framework, a target agent with a hidden motive interacts with other agents including one representing the user, who then consults the evaluated assistant to infer the target’s motive, providing verifiable ground truth by construction.
Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for everyday personal support and advice, yet evaluating their social reasoning in such consultation settings remains challenging since (1) it requires setups where the assistant learns about social situations from subjective user narratives, and (2) social properties, such as others’ intentions, typically lack verifiable ground truth.
Designed to address both of these challenges, we introduce an evaluation framework for social reasoning based on multi-agent simulations. In our framework, a target agent is assigned a hidden motive and interacts with other agents, including one representing the user. The user then consults with the evaluated assistant, which must infer the target's hidden motive. Evaluating a diverse range of LLMs through our framework reveals that relying on subjective user mediation substantially complicates social reasoning. Furthermore, models are sensitive to user framing, require more detail than humans need to reach correct predictions, and fail to fully leverage clarification questions. We open-source the framework and dataset to encourage future research on user-mediated social reasoning.
When evaluating LLMs’ social reasoning, it’s important to recognize that deployed assistants operate within a user-mediated reality. In classical reasoning tasks like math and code, LLMs operate over objective, complete information. However, when an LLM acts as a conversational assistant and is asked for personal support and advice, it does not observe the actual social interactions firsthand; its only source of information is the subjective, potentially biased lens of the user.
This information asymmetry can be challenging, as users may omit crucial context or provide a distorted narrative due to personal bias (e.g., projecting their insecurities onto their recounting of events). When models adopt the user's premise, they may amplify one-sided assumptions rather than offer objective assessment. This can result in an undesired failure mode, such as dispensing harsh advice against a colleague who was actually trying to help.
Existing evaluations often constrain their scope to edge-cases and overt anomalies, like testing whether models endorse absurd claims such as a human claiming to have supernatural powers, largely overlooking more nuanced everyday social interactions. These everyday interactions represent a massive share of real-world usage, translating to hundr
news.summary: Google Research has published a framework that evaluates large language models’ ability to understand social contexts through multi‑agent simulations. The study shows that LLMs struggle with user‑mediated narratives, highlighting gaps in social reasoning that could affect assistant reliability.

news.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
news.source_text:
Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.
One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.
We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.
Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.
The setup
The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):
- Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning.
- Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs (control → candidate → control). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics.
- Log every run in PLAN.md, including regressions and dead ends.
- Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner.

The model leverages a looped Mixture‑of‑Experts architecture and supports speculative decoding via DSpark, offering significant speedups on vLLM and SGLang.

news.source_text:

The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled.
iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis.
None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply.
“Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.”
Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle.
“Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.”
What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime.
“Teams can focus on solving their business problems and delegate execution to our platform.”
The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later.
“The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time.
The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable.
Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox.
“It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.”
The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS.
The model choice
news.summary: OpenAI’s Remote Agents Platform enables large-scale automated coding tasks across thousands of repositories via a REST API and isolated sandboxes, reportedly doubling vulnerability fixes at iFood. It demonstrates a new way to outsource code analysis and remediation to an AI-powered runtime, potentially reducing manual effort for massive codebases.

news.title: Backblaze explains why it's sharing customer information with advertisers
news.summary_raw: Backblaze tells Ars it won't share users' backup, storage files with advertisers.
news.source_text:
Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze’s privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.
Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.”
The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.
On December 1, a new privacy policy takes effect. It includes a table listing the types of “general personal information” that Backblaze says it has been collecting and sharing with third parties, including “advertising and marketing partners” since December 1, 2025, This information includes identifiers (such as “name, address, Internet Protocol address, [and] email address”); commercial information (such as “records of personal property, products or services purchased, obtained, or considered, or other purchasing or consuming histories or tendencies”; geolocation data that “can be used to determine a device’s physical location”; and “sensory or surveillance data” (which includes “call recordings or other audio, electronic, or visual monitoring or surveillance”).
This has concerned some users, but a Backblaze spokesperson told Ars Technica that “Backblaze does not sell or share sensory or surveillance data, such as call recordings, for targeted advertising, and we do not disclose it to advertising or marketing partners.” They added:
news.summary: Backblaze announced a policy change that now allows the company to share customer data, including personally identifying information, with advertising partners. The new privacy terms go into effect next month and raise significant concerns about data exposure for users.

news.title: From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity
news.summary_raw: Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra.
news.source_text:
From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity
Built in collaboration with analytical chemists and using community-developed tools, Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra, lay out chemical evidence, and match frontier-level retrieval accuracy even with a lightweight model.
Every sample of blood, soil or plant tissue contains a vast array of small molecules, such as nutrients, hormones, drugs and their breakdown products, pollutants, or bioactive compounds with therapeutic potential. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of these molecular signals in a single drop of sample extract, measuring the masses of charged molecules and, in tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), the fragments they break into.
These measurements, however, do not directly reveal the molecular structure. Researchers cannot immediately tell which compound produced a signal and relate it to its biological role or downstream use cases.
To fully map the diversity of small molecules, which remains largely uncharted, researchers need ways to translate mass spectra to molecular structures at scale. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra from previously measured molecules. Yet even after a decade of expanding reference libraries, spectral searches annotate on average only about 5% of measured spectra, and 10% for human samples; the rest has been called the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry.
Many of the molecules producing these unannotated signals are already listed in public chemical databases, but their spectra have not been recorded, so there is no reference spectrum to compare against. Elucidating them instead requires inferring the structure directly from the observed fragment ions.
Analytical chemists have a well-tested, step-by-step workflow for narrowing down candidate structures from tandem (MS/MS) spectra: check spectral reference libraries, find the molecular formula and retrieve candidate structures from chemical databases, and then test every candidate against observed fragment peaks.
The tools for each step exist and are openly available, but running the full workflow would take a domain expert a significant amount of time for every single spectrum. Because a single study can produce thousands of spectra, manual analysis cannot keep up, leaving most of these signals unannotated.
Today, we are sharing Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity, a suite of domain skills that pair Gemini's chemical reasoning with the ability to run established mass spectrometry tools and query public chemical databases on the user's behalf to fulfil their request. Antigravity runs these skills, combines their results, and reasons about the chemistry, laying out the evidence for a chemist to review.
For molecules that are already catalogued in a database, identification is much faster. For undiscovered molecules, the agent still helps: it narr
news.summary: Google DeepMind has released Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity, a set of domain skills that use Gemini’s chemical reasoning to interpret tandem mass spectra and suggest molecular structures. This tool automates the traditionally labor‑intensive workflow of matching spectra to databases and inferring structures, accelerating discovery in chemistry research.

news.title: An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
news.source_text:
CUGA Agent
Configurable Generalist Agent, leader in AppWorld Benchmark
Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.
We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.
A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:
If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.
CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:
agent.knowledge.search().The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.
audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio
Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.
Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.
Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.
The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.
Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.
A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:
OFF_TOPIC, and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast.You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:
Wa
news.summary: IBM Research’s open‑source CUGA harness now supports a multilingual voice agent that bridges regional language queries to English‑only knowledge bases. By integrating multilingual embeddings, the system can accurately retrieve relevant information across languages without manual translation.
news.enterprise_use: Check the CUGA Apps demo on Hugging Face Spaces to test how well a multilingual voice agent works with your own knowledge sources. If your organization collects non‑English content, evaluate adding a multilingual embedding model (e.g., intfloat/multilingual-e5-large) to improve retrieval accuracy before scaling.

news.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
news.source_text:
Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.
These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.
To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.
Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.
One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. news.summary: Hugging Face highlights ethical and safety concerns surrounding AI agents in scientific research, emphasizing the need for scientists to maintain responsibility over AI-assisted tasks such as literature review, data analysis, and lab protocols.

news.title: Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long
news.summary_raw: The “hardest remaining problem in classical physics” gets a boost from terabytes of crowdsourced data and new ways of using machine learning and AI.
news.source_text:
In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.
Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?
Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.
Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.
“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”
This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.
But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.
